summary: This memo describes how IANA can hand out protocol code points early, before the RFC that defines them is finished. It applies to registries using the policies Specification Required, RFC Required, IETF Review, or Standards Action. The goal is to let implementers test and deploy while a specification is still being completed.

eli5.summary: When a club is still writing its rulebook, people still need membership numbers to start playing. This lets numbers be handed out early, before the book is done.

questions: early iana allocation of code points
how to get a code point before an rfc is published
how long does a temporary code point last
how to request an early code point allocation
subtitle: How a draft can get IANA code points reserved before it becomes an RFC, without early implementers guessing values.

tldr.problem: Authors often pick seemingly unused code points for implementations built before an RFC exists, and those guesses may clash with what IANA later assigns.
tldr.mechanism: Working group chairs and Area Directors approve a request, and IANA allocates the code points as Temporary for one year, with at most one renewal unless the IESG agrees.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice that obsoletes RFC 4020 and applies only to IETF Stream documents.

today: RFC 7120 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 100) that obsoletes RFC 4020. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem with Guessing Code Points
sections.content:
Protocol specifications often need code points, values for objects, messages or other protocol entities that let implementations interoperate. Many are recorded in registries run by IANA. Policies such as "IETF Review" or "Standards Action" keep tight control, but they create a problem when implementation or deployment experience is wanted before the document becomes an RFC.

To break the deadlock, authors often choose seemingly unused values, often the next available one. These may differ from what IANA later assigns, so early implementations will not interoperate with standard ones. Or IANA may assign a value for one extension while a pre-RFC implementation of a different extension picked the same one, causing a collision in the field.

The memo notes that for Routing Area working group documents, a pre-RFC implementation is highly desirable and sometimes even required (RFC 4794).
sections.eli5: If kids pick their own locker numbers before the school hands them out, two kids may pick the same one. It is better if the school lends numbers early.

sections.title: Which Registries and Documents Qualify
sections.content:
Early allocation applies only to registries whose policy, defined in RFC 5226, is "Specification Required" (where an RFC is the stable reference), "RFC Required", "IETF Review" or "Standards Action". It is intended only for IETF Stream documents. This memo obsoletes RFC 4020 and extends the kinds of registries that can qualify.

Policies such as "First Come First Served" or "Expert Review" do not need a formal IETF action before allocation, so they are outside what this memo addresses.
sections.eli5: This only works for the lists where grown-ups must approve each entry. Lists where anyone can sign up already work fine.

sections.title: Conditions for Early Allocation
sections.content:
IANA will consider a request only when all of these hold:

  • The code points come from an "RFC Required", "IETF Review" or "Standards Action" space, or from a "Specification Required" registry where the specification will be published as an RFC.
  • The format, semantics and processing rules are adequately described in an Internet-Draft.
  • The specification is stable: if it changes, implementations of the earlier and later versions must still interoperate seamlessly.
  • The Working Group chairs and Area Directors judge that there is sufficient community interest in early implementation and deployment, or that failing to allocate might lead to contention for the code point in the field.
sections.eli5: To borrow a number early, the plan must be written down, it must not change in ways that break things, and the grown-ups must agree people really want to try it.

sections.title: Request, Follow-Up and Expiry
sections.content:
The request goes through six steps. The authors ask the Working Group chairs, who check the conditions (especially stability and interest) and gauge WG consensus. The chairs then ask the Area Director(s) for approval, and the ADs may apply judgement, particularly if the registry might run out. If they approve, the chairs ask IANA, which allocates the value marked Temporary, valid for one year. The date of first allocation and the expiry date are recorded publicly. Drafts should not include a specific code point value until IANA has completed the early allocation. Where a document is not from a working group, the Shepherding Area Director replaces the WG chairs.

Authors and chairs must keep checking that changes remain backward compatible. If an incompatible change is needed, they must decide whether the old code points should be deprecated, weighing existing deployments. When the document reaches the point where IANA normally allocates, the authors and chairs remind IANA of the early allocations, and the Temporary tag is simply removed.

If an allocation expires first, the process may be repeated to renew it. At most one renewal request may be made. Further renewals need review by the IESG, with reasons and the WG's plans. An expired allocation stays visible in the registry; the chairs tell IANA to mark it deprecated, meaning it is not allocated and not available for a future document. Chairs may later let IANA de-allocate it fully. Implementers should treat an expired early allocation as deprecated. IANA is not responsible for tracking status or expiry. Allocations that are valid when a document is submitted to the IESG are not considered expired while it is under IESG consideration or awaiting publication in the RFC Editor's queue.
sections.eli5: A borrowed number is stamped with a date a year away. If the book is done in time, the stamp is removed. If not, you may ask once more. After that the number goes into the 'do not use' pile.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo removes the need for registries to be marked as specifically allowing early allocation, and IANA has removed such markings.

The security discussion concerns denial-of-service attacks on IANA: depletion of code space by early allocations and overloading IANA's process. IANA may at any time ask the IESG to suspend the procedures. There is also a concern that the process could be used as an end-run around the IETF process to get an allocation when an RFC will not be published, for example for a particular company or another standards body. The requirement for Area Director consent is described as an important safeguard.
sections.eli5: People could try to grab lots of numbers or use the loan trick to skip the rules. The grown-up approval step and IANA's ability to pause the program are the guards against that.
